<reason>PRO built a clean causal case—shrinkflation exists as a strategy only because the gram count is not read at the shelf—and then extracted from CON's own [B2.2] the admission that firms shrink to preserve price points shoppers anchor on. CON never squarely neutralized that; [B4.1] effectively conceded the two disclosures differ in salience while retreating to a memory-symmetry point that PRO had already answered (the sticker is the number actively read and compared against rivals). CON landed real hits—the store-vs-SKU churn distinction, the baseline question, the composite-delta ambiguity, and the exploitation of PRO's stray "was $3.49" concession into a "different proposal" charge—but PRO's fixes (two-line flag, previous regular size, safe harbour) stay within the motion's text and were answered directly under A1:/A2:. CON's strongest slogan ("fine print cannot be rescued by more of it") was undercut by PRO's point that a temporary flag at the sticker changes appearance, unlike permanent fine print. PRO also tracked CON's shifting objections persuasively. CON's late clarification that unit pricing is acceptable was honest but came only in closing. Both sides suffered similar clipping costs. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A2.1]-[A2.2] exposing the tension between "already disclosed in plain ink" and "so frequent it wallpapers the aisle," then arguing the existence of shrinkflation is the market's own verdict that disclosure fails—reinforced by seizing CON's [B2.2] anchoring admission in [A4.1] and [A5.1]. CON's [B2.1] SKU-vs-store answer was the best counter but left the anchoring concession standing.</best_rebuttal>
